Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Fractional optimal control of hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans
papers.abstract: This paper studies a fractional optimal control problem for a hantavirus transmission model involving interactions between rodent reservoirs and human populations. The model is formulated through a modified SIR–SIR structure, where both humans and rodents are divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. The classical integer-order model is extended by using the Caputo fractional derivative, which captures memory and hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three time-dependent control variables are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established to guarantee the biological and mathematical validity of the model. An optimal control problem is then formulated to minimize infected humans, infected rodents, and the costs of intervention. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin’s maximum principle for fractional systems. The adjoint equations, transversality conditions, and explicit characterization of the optimal controls are obtained. A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.

A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.

full_text_sections.abstract: This paper studies a fractional optimal control problem for a hantavirus transmission model involving interactions between rodent reservoirs and human populations. The model is formulated through a modified SIR–SIR structure, where both humans and rodents are divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. The classical integer-order model is extended by using the Caputo fractional derivative, which captures memory and hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three time-dependent control variables are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established to guarantee the biological and mathematical validity of the model. An optimal control problem is then formulated to minimize infected humans, infected rodents, and the costs of intervention. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin’s maximum principle for fractional systems. The adjoint equations, transversality conditions, and explicit characterization of the optimal controls are obtained. A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.

analysis_zh.background: 本文研究了针对涉及啮齿动物储宿主与人群相互作用的 汉坦病毒 传播模型的分数阶最优控制问题。
analysis_zh.methods: 在人体和啮齿动物的改进 SIR–SIR 结构中引入 Caputo 分数阶导数以捕获记忆效应;设定三项时变控制(啮齿动物扑杀、环境卫生、感染人群治疗);通过分数阶系统的 Pontryagin 最大值原理推导必要的最优性条件;采用分数阶 Adams–Bashforth–Moulton 预测‐校正方法结合前向‐后向扫描算法进行数值求解。

analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了一个理论框架,展示分数阶动力学和最优控制如何为 汉坦病毒 管理提供依据,强调记忆效应在疾病建模和干预设计中的作用。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该模型在进行特定疫情预测前需使用相匹配的人类和啮齿动物监测数据进行经验校准和验证,且证据仅限于摘要。

papers.title: Current State of Diagnostics of Hemorrhagic Fevers Caused by Viruses of the Genera Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus and Orthoflavivirus, Using the LAMP Method
papers.abstract: The work is an overview of the data on application of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the diagnosis of viral hemorrhagic fevers caused by pathogens belonging to the second pathogenicity group. The first part of the review provides a brief characterization of the main viral agents of hemorrhagic fevers from the families Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae, and Flaviviridae. Special attention is given to the epidemiological significance of these pathogens and the challenges associated with their timely laboratory identification. The aim of the study was to analyze and systematize the data available in the literature sources on the use of LAMP as an alternative to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for diagnosing hemorrhagic fevers caused by these agents. The review considers the principal methods for registering LAMP results, including the turbidimetric method, immunochromatographic assays, the use of fluorescent dyes, metal-based indicators and pH-sensitive dyes. A comparative analysis of the analytical characteristics of existing LAMP reagent kits for each of the described agents is also presented. It is noted that there are currently no registered and widely available commercial LAMP reagent kits for detecting the genetic markers of these viruses. This underscores the need for further research, since the implementation of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods suitable for field use is a prerequisite for effective epidemic control measures. Therefore, the development of appropriate reagent kits based on the LAMP method represents a promising objective.

papers.full_text: Современное состояние диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых вирусами родов Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus и Orthoflavivirus методом LAMP https://doi.org/10.21055/0370-1069-2026-3-6-15 Аннотация Представлен обзор данных о применении метода петлевой изотермической амплификации (loop mediated isothermal amplification, LAMP) для диагностики вирусных геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых возбудителями, относящимися к II группе патогенности. Дана краткая характеристика основных вирусных возбудителей геморрагических лихорадок из семейств Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae и Flaviviridae. Особое внимание уделено эпидемиологической значимости данных патогенов и сложности их своевременной лабораторной идентификации. Основная цель работы заключалась в анализе и систематизации имеющихся в литературе данных об использовании метода LAMP как альтернативы ПЦР для диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых данными возбудителями. Рассмотрены основные методы детекции результатов LAMP, включая турбидиметрический метод, иммунохроматографический анализ, использование флуоресцентных красителей, металлоиндикаторов и pH-чувствительных красителей. Проведен сравнительный анализ аналитических характеристик разработанных наборов реагентов для LAMP-диагностики каждого из рассматриваемых возбудителей. Отмечается, что в настоящее время не существует зарегистрированных и широкодоступных коммерческих LAMP-наборов реагентов для выявления генетических маркеров данных вирусов. Это актуализирует необходимость дальнейших исследований, так как внедрение быстрых и надежных методов диагностики, пригодных для использования в полевых условиях, является необходимым условием эффективных противоэпидемических мероприятий. Таким образом, разработка соответствующих наборов реагентов на основе метода LAMP представляет собой перспективную задачу. Об авторах К. Р. full_text_sections.full_text: Современное состояние диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых вирусами родов Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus и Orthoflavivirus методом LAMP https://doi.org/10.21055/0370-1069-2026-3-6-15 Аннотация Представлен обзор данных о применении метода петлевой изотермической амплификации (loop mediated isothermal amplification, LAMP) для диагностики вирусных геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых возбудителями, относящимися к II группе патогенности. Дана краткая характеристика основных вирусных возбудителей геморрагических лихорадок из семейств Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae и Flaviviridae. Особое внимание уделено эпидемиологической значимости данных патогенов и сложности их своевременной лабораторной идентификации. Основная цель работы заключалась в анализе и систематизации имеющихся в литературе данных об использовании метода LAMP как альтернативы ПЦР для диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых данными возбудителями. Рассмотрены основные методы детекции результатов LAMP, включая турбидиметрический метод, иммунохроматографический анализ, использование флуоресцентных красителей, металлоиндикаторов и pH-чувствительных красителей. Проведен сравнительный анализ аналитических характеристик разработанных наборов реагентов для LAMP-диагностики каждого из рассматриваемых возбудителей. Отмечается, что в настоящее время не существует зарегистрированных и широкодоступных коммерческих LAMP-наборов реагентов для выявления генетических маркеров данных вирусов. Это актуализирует необходимость дальнейших исследований, так как внедрение быстрых и надежных методов диагностики, пригодных для использования в полевых условиях, является необходимым условием эффективных противоэпидемических мероприятий. Таким образом, разработка соответствующих наборов реагентов на основе метода LAMP представляет собой перспективную задачу. Об авторах К. Р. papers.title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus and poses a potential threat to human health. Current detection methods based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays for other hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) may carry the risk of false negatives. This study aims to address the technical bottlenecks of low accuracy and insufficient sensitivity in current detection of DBSV. RESULTS: We developed a signal amplification strategy mediated by a photoactivated magnetic 3D DNA walker, which enables light-controllable fluorescence detection. Specifically, this fluorescence sensing platform introduces the catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) technique for dual signal amplification. This system requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA. Then, exonuclease III (Exo III) provides propulsion for the walking process to release a specific trigger strand, subsequently activating the CHA cycle and producing a fluorescent signal. Experimental results confirm that the system displays excellent selectivity and anti-interference ability, successfully distinguishing target sequences with single-base mismatch (SBM), double-base mismatch (DBM), and triple-base mismatch (TBM). Furthermore, the platform achieves a DBSV-RNA detection limit (LOD) of 30 fM with a linear range spanning 10-1-106 pM. The applicability of the method has been rigorously validated using human serum specimens. SIGNIFICANCE: This study provides a novel strategy for the application of spatiotemporally controllable DNA walkers in RNA detection, demonstrating considerable potential for early viral diagnosis and field monitoring.

papers.title: The Potential Risk Factors of Hantavirus Transmission to Humans from Infected Rodents in Malaysia
papers.abstract: Zoonotic hantavirus is a negative single-stranded RNA virus from the family Bunyaviridae which is known to cause two significant rodent-borne diseases in humans namely hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), affecting about 30 000 people worldwide each year. HFRS is a disease found endemically in Asia and Europe with case fatality rates varying from <1% to 12%, while HPS which has a higher mortality rate of approximately 40% occurs within the American continent. Many countries in Southeast Asia unaware the public health implication of Hantavirus infection despite favorable ecological conditions include rich rodent species diversity, urbanisation and high human-wildlife interface that serve as ecological condition that could support the virus persistence and transmission.Since humans serve as spillover hosts who are infected largely by inhalation of infected rodents’ excreta, it is crucial to fill in the research gap by identifying the risk factors for human hantavirus infection. This paper provides a review of the potential risk factors associated with hantavirus transmission to humans from infected rodents in Malaysia focusing on behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental. Other pieces of knowledge such as hantavirus virological properties, the geographical distribution with its respective role as a reservoir, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, particularly its propensity to be misclassified due to mimic symptom with dengue and leptospirosis. To effectively mitigate transmission, Malaysia must transition from a fragmented surveillance model to a proactive, integrated One Health framework that bridges the inter-governmental agencies through a unified data-sharing platform to monitor active viral strains and prevent localised spillover outbreaks.

Many countries in Southeast Asia unaware the public health implication of Hantavirus infection despite favorable ecological conditions include rich rodent species diversity, urbanisation and high human-wildlife interface that serve as ecological condition that could support the virus persistence and transmission.Since humans serve as spillover hosts who are infected largely by inhalation of infected rodents’ excreta, it is crucial to fill in the research gap by identifying the risk factors for human hantavirus infection. This paper provides a review of the potential risk factors associated with hantavirus transmission to humans from infected rodents in Malaysia focusing on behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental. Other pieces of knowledge such as hantavirus virological properties, the geographical distribution with its respective role as a reservoir, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, particularly its propensity to be misclassified due to mimic symptom with dengue and leptospirosis. To effectively mitigate transmission, Malaysia must transition from a fragmented surveillance model to a proactive, integrated One Health framework that bridges the inter-governmental agencies through a unified data-sharing platform to monitor active viral strains and prevent localised spillover outbreaks.

full_text_sections.abstract: Zoonotic hantavirus is a negative single-stranded RNA virus from the family Bunyaviridae which is known to cause two significant rodent-borne diseases in humans namely hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), affecting about 30 000 people worldwide each year. HFRS is a disease found endemically in Asia and Europe with case fatality rates varying from <1% to 12%, while HPS which has a higher mortality rate of approximately 40% occurs within the American continent. Many countries in Southeast Asia unaware the public health implication of Hantavirus infection despite favorable ecological conditions include rich rodent species diversity, urbanisation and high human-wildlife interface that serve as ecological condition that could support the virus persistence and transmission.Since humans serve as spillover hosts who are infected largely by inhalation of infected rodents’ excreta, it is crucial to fill in the research gap by identifying the risk factors for human hantavirus infection. This paper provides a review of the potential risk factors associated with hantavirus transmission to humans from infected rodents in Malaysia focusing on behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental. Other pieces of knowledge such as hantavirus virological properties, the geographical distribution with its respective role as a reservoir, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, particularly its propensity to be misclassified due to mimic symptom with dengue and leptospirosis. analysis.background: Zoonotic hantavirus is a negative‑sense RNA virus causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), affecting about 30 000 people worldwide each year; HFRS has case‑fatality rates <1%–12% in Asia/Europe, while HPS has ~40% mortality in the Americas. Southeast Asian countries, including Malaysia, have ecological conditions (diverse rodents, urbanisation, high human‑wildlife interface) that could support virus persistence, yet public‑health implications are poorly recognised.
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: The review identifies behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental factors as potential risk drivers for hantavirus transmission from infected rodents to humans in Malaysia.
analysis.contribution: It synthesises knowledge on hantavirus virology, distribution, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, and recommends moving from fragmented surveillance to a proactive, integrated One Health framework for monitoring viral strains and preventing spillover.
analysis.limitations: The paper is presented as an abstract‑only review, providing no detailed methodology, primary data, or quantitative analysis.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes HFRS and HPS, affecting ~30,000 people annually with notable fatality rates, and Malaysia's ecological setting may favour transmission yet risks are understudied. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: The review highlights behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental factors as potential drivers of rodent‑to‑human transmission in Malaysia. Contribution: It compiles virological, ecological, and clinical insights and urges a shift to an integrated One Health surveillance system. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, lacking detailed methods and primary data.

papers.title: In Silico Prediction and Structural Mapping of Linear B-Cell Epitopes in Andes Virus Glycoprotein as Potential Vaccine Candidates
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. This study aimed to identify and structurally map linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein using an immunoinformatics-based approach. The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt, and linear B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 3.0 with a threshold of 0.030. Candidate peptides were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Five preliminary epitope candidates were identified, among which E1, E2, E3, and E4 met the antigenicity criterion. The refined structure showed favorable validation parameters, with an ERRAT score of 97.73 and 97.88% of residues in the favored Ramachandran region. Structural mapping indicated that E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) were positioned on exposed surface regions, supporting their prioritization as the most promising candidates. E4 (PSTSSTDT) also showed potential, whereas E3 (HPRGEDHD), despite having the highest antigenicity score, appeared less structurally exposed. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates in ANDV glycoprotein. However, experimental validation is required to confirm their immunological relevance.

papers.full_text: Volume 1 (2026) h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.7 SHORT COMMUNICATION Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya In Silico Prediction and Structural Mapping of Candidate Linear B-Cell Epitopes in Andes Virus Glycoprotein Husaina Kunii Nariswari1, Moh. Royhan Afnani1,3, Muhammad Fajrul Adi Syahputra1, Rangga Adhi Prastika2,3, Abdul Rahman Siregar1* 1Department of Biology, Faculty of Biology, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, 55281, Indonesia 2Department of Nanotechnology Engineering, Faculty of Advanced Technology and Multidiscipline, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya 60115, Indonesia. 3Drug and Vaccine Innovation Research Group, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Surabaya, Indonesia *Corresponding author: ar.siregar@ugm.ac.id ARTICLE HISTORY Received: 16 Jun 2026 Revised: 21 Jul 2026 Accepted: 29 Jul 2026 Published: 30 Sep 2026 ABSTRACT Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. This study aimed to identify and prioritize candidate linear B-cell epitopes in the ANDV glycoprotein using an integrated immunoinformatics approach. The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt, and linear B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 3.0 with a threshold of 0.030. Candidate peptides were evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Surface-localized candidates were further assessed through molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure using ClusPro 2.0, followed by binding free energy estimation using PRODIGY. E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE), E2 (QTKTVNLRGT), and E4 (PSTSSTDT) showed favorable antigenicity, non-allergenic and non-toxic profiles, and surface localization on the glycoprotein model. Docking analysis further supported their prioritization, with predicted binding free energies of -10.0, -9.4, and -9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2, and E4, respectively. Overall, E1 emerged as the strongest candidate, while E2 and E4 represent additional candidates for further validation. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for candidate linear B-cell epitopes in ANDV glycoprotein, although experimental confirmation remains necessary. Keywords: Andes virus; B-cell epitope; glycoprotein; immunoinformatics; structural mapping; candidate linear B-cell epitope Introduction A recent cluster of Andes virus infections associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius has heightened international concern regarding the public health significance of pathogenic orthohantaviruses (Koopmans et al., 2026). Andes virus (ANDV), a zoonotic pathogen within the genus Orthohantavirus and family Hantaviridae, typically infects humans through inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodent reservoirs. Notably, ANDV is epidemiologically unique due to documented instances of limited person-to- person transmission, particularly among close contacts (Chediack et al., 2026; Martinez- Valdebenito et al., 2014). This transmission feature, combined with its association with severe cardiopulmonary disease, underscores the importance of ANDV for public health surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and vaccine development. ANDV is a primary etiological agent of hantavirus Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease marked by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory failure, and cardiogenic shock (Warner et al., 2025). While the incidence of HCPS is generally lower than that of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Old World hantaviruses, HCPS exhibits a substantially higher case-fatality rate, typically reported at 30–40% (Angulo et al., 2017; Barrera et al., 2025; Quarleri et al., 2026). Despite the clinical severity of ANDV infection, no specific antiviral therapy or widely approved vaccine is currently available for human use. This lack of medical countermeasures is particularly concerning given ecological disturbances, climate variability, and habitat changes that may influence rodent population dynamics and elevate the risk of human exposure to infected reservoirs (Moirano et al., 2024). Structurally, ANDV is an enveloped, negative- sense RNA virus with a tripartite genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments. The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, the medium segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into Gn and Gc, and the large segment encodes the RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (Beltrán-Ortiz et al., 2017). The envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc are of particular interest for vaccine development because they are displayed on the virion surface and mediate host-cell attachment, receptor engagement, endocytic entry, and membrane fusion. Their surface exposure facilitates antibody recognition, supporting their selection as antigenic targets for epitope-based vaccine research (Banerjee & Mukhopadhyay, 2016; Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014). B-cell epitopes are specific antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and contribute to humoral immune responses (Caoili, 2022). In vaccine design, identifying B-cell epitopes is essential because antibody-mediated immunity and immunological memory are critical for protection against viral reinfection. Linear B-cell epitopes are particularly valuable in immunoinformatics-based screening, as they can be derived from the primary amino acid sequence, assessed for antigenicity and safety, and mapped onto three-dimensional antigen structures (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). However, sequence-based prediction alone does not adequately determine biological accessibility or immunogenic potential. Structural mapping is therefore required to establish whether predicted epitopes are located on solvent-exposed regions of the target protein, where they are more likely to be accessible to antibody binding (Afnani & Purnama, 2025; Francino-Urdaniz & Whitehead, 2021). Although B-cell epitope prediction, multiepitope vaccine design, and structural evaluation have been applied in viral vaccine- related studies, including hantavirus targets, most previous hantavirus immunoinformatics studies have emphasized broad whole-proteome screening or multiepitope vaccine construct design rather than a focused prioritization of linear B-cell epitopes derived specifically from the ANDV glycoprotein (Abdulla et al., 2021). The novelty of the present study therefore does not rely on the use of individual computational tools, which are well-established in immunoinformatics research, but on the ANDV- specific integration of linear B-cell epitope prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure for candidate prioritization. This integrated approach allows predicted epitopes to be evaluated not only on the basis of sequence-level epitope propensity, but also according to their predicted antigenicity, safety profile, structural localization, and interaction potential with an antigen-recognition model. Such a focused framework is particularly relevant for glycoprotein antigens, in which not all sequence- predicted epitopes are necessarily exposed or available for antibody recognition on the folded protein surface. Therefore, this study aimed to identify and prioritize linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein through an integrated immunoinformatics approach combining sequence-based prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure. Candidate epitopes were further assessed for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, structural localization, and predicted BCR-binding affinity. The results provide preliminary computational evidence for prioritized surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates that may inform future experimental evaluation for Andes virus vaccine-associated or diagnostic applications. However, as this study is Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya entirely computational, the predicted epitopes should be regarded as potential candidates requiring further experimental validation through in vitro and in vivo studies. Materials and Methods Retrieval and Curation of Andes Virus Glycoprotein Sequence The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from the UniProt Knowledgebase using the taxonomic identifier and protein accession as search criteria. The UniProt entry Q9E006, annotated as ANDV glycoprotein and consisting of 1138 amino acids, was selected as the reference sequence for downstream analysis (Shimizu et al., 2013). The FASTA sequence and associated metadata, including accession number, organism name, protein length, and database source, were recorded to ensure sequence traceability and reproducibility. UniProtKB provides curated protein sequence and functional annotation resources, supporting its use as a primary source for protein sequence retrieval. Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction Linear B-cell epitope prediction was performed using BepiPred 3.0, a sequence-based epitope prediction tool developed for identifying residues with potential B-cell epitope propensity (Clifford et al., 2022). The higher-confidence prediction option was selected. In this study, a threshold of ≥0.030 was used as a sequence-specific operational cutoff based on the score distribution observed across the ANDV glycoprotein. This cutoff was selected to balance epitope recovery and prediction stringency. Higher cutoff values retained only a very limited number of short epitope regions and reduced the ability to capture biologically plausible contiguous peptide segments, whereas lower cutoff values increased the inclusion of low-scoring regions that may represent less reliable predictions. Antigenicity, Allergenicity, and Toxicity Screening The predicted linear B-cell epitope candidates were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity. Antigenicity was assessed using VaxiJen v2.0 with a threshold value of 0.400; peptides with antigenicity scores above this threshold were considered potentially antigenic (Afnani, Kharisma, et al., 2026). VaxiJen is an alignment-independent antigen prediction server that classifies antigens based on the physicochemical properties of protein sequences (Doytchinova & Flower, 2007). Allergenicity was predicted using AllerTOP v2.1, and only peptides classified as non-allergenic were retained. AllerTOP is an alignment-free allergenicity prediction server based on physicochemical properties and machine-learning classification (Dimitrov et al., 2014). Toxicity was evaluated using ToxinPred, and peptides predicted as non-toxic were prioritized for further structural mapping. ToxinPred is designed to classify peptides as toxic or non-toxic based on computational sequence-derived features (Rathore et al., 2024). Prediction, Refinement, and 3D Structure Validation The three-dimensional (3D) structure of the Andes virus glycoprotein was predicted using the AlphaFold Server (Kovalevskiy et al., 2024; Prastika et al., 2026). The predicted structure was then refined using the GalaxyWEB server to improve local structural geometry and reduce potential modeling artifacts. The refined model was validated using structure quality assessment parameters (Ko et al., 2012). The ERRAT score was calculated using the Structure Validation Server, and stereochemical quality was assessed using Ramachandran plot analysis through RamPlot (Afnani, Emilia, et al., 2026; Laskowski et al., 2013). The validated model was subsequently used as the structural template for mapping the selected linear B-cell epitope candidates. Structural Mapping and Visualization of Linear B-Cell Epitope Candidates The selected linear B-cell epitope candidates were mapped onto the refined 3D structure of the ANDV glycoprotein using PyMOL under an academic license. Epitope positions were identified based on their amino acid coordinates in the full-length glycoprotein sequence and visualized on the 3D model using distinct colors. Both cartoon and surface representations were generated to assess the spatial distribution and surface exposure of each candidate epitope (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Epitope candidates located on surface-exposed regions were prioritized because B-cell epitopes are more likely to be accessible to antibody recognition when positioned on the external surface of the antigen. In contrast, epitopes located within Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya buried, transmembrane, or structurally uncertain regions were interpreted with caution and were not prioritized for further analysis. Molecular Docking with B-Cell ReceptorThe prioritized linear B-cell epitopes, were further evaluated through molecular docking with the B- cell receptor (BCR). The BCR structure was obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank using PDB ID 5IFH (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Molecular docking was performed using the ClusPro 2.0, with BCR designated as the receptor and each epitope peptide as the ligand (Arapa et al., 2026). The best-ranked docking complex from each epitope-BCR interaction was selected for further evaluation. The predicted binding free energy (ΔG) of each complex was then assessed using the PRODIGY web server, where more negative ΔG values indicate stronger predicted binding affinity (Xue et al., 2016). The resulting docking complexes were visualized using PyMOL to examine the interaction orientation and spatial positioning of each epitope on the BCR surface. full_text_sections.full_text: Volume 1 (2026) h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.7 SHORT COMMUNICATION Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya In Silico Prediction and Structural Mapping of Candidate Linear B-Cell Epitopes in Andes Virus Glycoprotein Husaina Kunii Nariswari1, Moh. Royhan Afnani1,3, Muhammad Fajrul Adi Syahputra1, Rangga Adhi Prastika2,3, Abdul Rahman Siregar1* 1Department of Biology, Faculty of Biology, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, 55281, Indonesia 2Department of Nanotechnology Engineering, Faculty of Advanced Technology and Multidiscipline, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya 60115, Indonesia. 3Drug and Vaccine Innovation Research Group, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Surabaya, Indonesia *Corresponding author: ar.siregar@ugm.ac.id ARTICLE HISTORY Received: 16 Jun 2026 Revised: 21 Jul 2026 Accepted: 29 Jul 2026 Published: 30 Sep 2026 ABSTRACT Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. This study aimed to identify and prioritize candidate linear B-cell epitopes in the ANDV glycoprotein using an integrated immunoinformatics approach. The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt, and linear B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 3.0 with a threshold of 0.030. Candidate peptides were evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Surface-localized candidates were further assessed through molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure using ClusPro 2.0, followed by binding free energy estimation using PRODIGY. E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE), E2 (QTKTVNLRGT), and E4 (PSTSSTDT) showed favorable antigenicity, non-allergenic and non-toxic profiles, and surface localization on the glycoprotein model. Docking analysis further supported their prioritization, with predicted binding free energies of -10.0, -9.4, and -9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2, and E4, respectively. Overall, E1 emerged as the strongest candidate, while E2 and E4 represent additional candidates for further validation. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for candidate linear B-cell epitopes in ANDV glycoprotein, although experimental confirmation remains necessary. Keywords: Andes virus; B-cell epitope; glycoprotein; immunoinformatics; structural mapping; candidate linear B-cell epitope Introduction A recent cluster of Andes virus infections associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius has heightened international concern regarding the public health significance of pathogenic orthohantaviruses (Koopmans et al., 2026). Andes virus (ANDV), a zoonotic pathogen within the genus Orthohantavirus and family Hantaviridae, typically infects humans through inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodent reservoirs. Notably, ANDV is epidemiologically unique due to documented instances of limited person-to- person transmission, particularly among close contacts (Chediack et al., 2026; Martinez- Valdebenito et al., 2014). This transmission feature, combined with its association with severe cardiopulmonary disease, underscores the importance of ANDV for public health surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and vaccine development. ANDV is a primary etiological agent of hantavirus Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease marked by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory failure, and cardiogenic shock (Warner et al., 2025). While the incidence of HCPS is generally lower than that of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Old World hantaviruses, HCPS exhibits a substantially higher case-fatality rate, typically reported at 30–40% (Angulo et al., 2017; Barrera et al., 2025; Quarleri et al., 2026). Despite the clinical severity of ANDV infection, no specific antiviral therapy or widely approved vaccine is currently available for human use. This lack of medical countermeasures is particularly concerning given ecological disturbances, climate variability, and habitat changes that may influence rodent population dynamics and elevate the risk of human exposure to infected reservoirs (Moirano et al., 2024). Structurally, ANDV is an enveloped, negative- sense RNA virus with a tripartite genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments. The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, the medium segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into Gn and Gc, and the large segment encodes the RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (Beltrán-Ortiz et al., 2017). The envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc are of particular interest for vaccine development because they are displayed on the virion surface and mediate host-cell attachment, receptor engagement, endocytic entry, and membrane fusion. Their surface exposure facilitates antibody recognition, supporting their selection as antigenic targets for epitope-based vaccine research (Banerjee & Mukhopadhyay, 2016; Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014). B-cell epitopes are specific antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and contribute to humoral immune responses (Caoili, 2022). In vaccine design, identifying B-cell epitopes is essential because antibody-mediated immunity and immunological memory are critical for protection against viral reinfection. Linear B-cell epitopes are particularly valuable in immunoinformatics-based screening, as they can be derived from the primary amino acid sequence, assessed for antigenicity and safety, and mapped onto three-dimensional antigen structures (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). However, sequence-based prediction alone does not adequately determine biological accessibility or immunogenic potential. Structural mapping is therefore required to establish whether predicted epitopes are located on solvent-exposed regions of the target protein, where they are more likely to be accessible to antibody binding (Afnani & Purnama, 2025; Francino-Urdaniz & Whitehead, 2021). Although B-cell epitope prediction, multiepitope vaccine design, and structural evaluation have been applied in viral vaccine- related studies, including hantavirus targets, most previous hantavirus immunoinformatics studies have emphasized broad whole-proteome screening or multiepitope vaccine construct design rather than a focused prioritization of linear B-cell epitopes derived specifically from the ANDV glycoprotein (Abdulla et al., 2021). The novelty of the present study therefore does not rely on the use of individual computational tools, which are well-established in immunoinformatics research, but on the ANDV- specific integration of linear B-cell epitope prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure for candidate prioritization. This integrated approach allows predicted epitopes to be evaluated not only on the basis of sequence-level epitope propensity, but also according to their predicted antigenicity, safety profile, structural localization, and interaction potential with an antigen-recognition model. Such a focused framework is particularly relevant for glycoprotein antigens, in which not all sequence- predicted epitopes are necessarily exposed or available for antibody recognition on the folded protein surface. analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with severe outcomes and no broadly approved human vaccine, representing a public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt and linear B‑cell epitopes were predicted with BepiPred 3.0 (threshold 0.030); candidate peptides were screened for antigenicity, allergenicity and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1 and ToxinPred; a 3‑D glycoprotein model was built with AlphaFold, refined by GalaxyWEB and validated (ERRAT, Ramachandran); surface‑exposed epitopes were further docked to a B‑cell receptor using ClusPro 2.0 with binding free energies estimated by PRODIGY.
analysis.results: Five preliminary epitopes were identified, of which E1, E2, E3 and E4 met antigenicity criteria; the refined model showed an ERRAT score of 97.73 % and 97.88 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions; structural mapping placed E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) on exposed surfaces, E4 (PSTSSTDT) also surface‑accessible, while E3 (HPRGEDHD) was less exposed; docking yielded predicted binding free energies of –10.0, –9.4 and –9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2 and E4 respectively, with E1 emerging as the strongest candidate.
analysis.contribution: The study provides preliminary computational evidence for surface‑accessible linear B‑cell epitopes in the ANDV glycoprotein, offering candidate targets for future vaccine design and serological tool development.
analysis.limitations: All findings are based on in‑silico predictions; experimental validation of antigenicity, immunogenicity and protective efficacy is required.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes severe cardiopulmonary syndrome and lacks approved vaccines, posing a public‑health threat. Methods: Researchers retrieved the ANDV glycoprotein sequence, predicted linear B‑cell epitopes with BepiPred, screened them for antigenicity, allergenicity and toxicity, modeled the protein with AlphaFold, refined and validated the structure, and docked surface‑exposed epitopes to a B‑cell receptor. Results: Five epitopes were found, four met antigenicity criteria; the model showed high validation scores, and E1 and E2 were surface‑exposed with favorable docking energies (–10.0, –9.4 kcal/mol), making E1 the top candidate. Contribution: Provides computationally identified epitope candidates for ANDV vaccine research. Limitations: Results are purely computational and need experimental confirmation.

papers.title: Transmisión interpersonal del virus Andes: revisión narrativa de la evidencia actual y sus implicaciones clínicas
papers.abstract: Los hantavirus constituyen un grupo de virus responsables de zoonosis emergentes transmitidas principalmente por roedores. El virus Andes (ANDV), endémico de Sudamérica, constituye una excepción dentro de este grupo viral debido a la evidencia de transmisión interpersonal limitada. El objetivo de esta revisión narrativa es actualizar la evidencia disponible sobre la transmisión humano-humano del ANDV y analizar sus implicaciones clínicas y epidemiológicas. Se realizó una búsqueda bibliográfica narrativa en PubMed/MEDLINE y Google Scholar, incluyendo estudios epidemiológicos, revisiones y trabajos experimentales relevantes. Los brotes descritos en Argentina y Chile, junto con estudios moleculares y modelos animales, apoyan la existencia de transmisión interpersonal en contextos de contacto estrecho y prolongado, especialmente durante fases iniciales de la enfermedad. La detección de ARN viral en saliva y secreciones respiratorias aporta plausibilidad biológica a este fenómeno. La capacidad de transmisión interpersonal del ANDV posee implicaciones relevantes para el aislamiento, el rastreo de contactos y la vigilancia epidemiológica en áreas endémicas. Hantaviruses constitute a group of viruses responsible for emerging zoonotic diseases primarily transmitted by rodents. Andes virus (ANDV), endemic to South America, is unique among hantaviruses because of evidence supporting limited person-to-person transmission. The aim of this narrative review is to summarize current evidence regarding interpersonal transmission of ANDV and its clinical and epidemiological implications. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar including epidemiological studies, reviews, and experimental reports. Outbreaks described in Argentina and Chile, together with molecular studies and animal models, support the existence of person-to-person transmission in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly during the early stages of disease. Detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions provides biological plausibility for this phenomenon. The transmissibility of ANDV has relevant implications for patient isolation, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance in endemic regions.

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. Importance The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown.
