A broadly reactive antibody 56 neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein 57 surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown. 58 59 Introduction 60 Entry of enveloped viruses into host cells is a major determinant of tissue tropism and 61 cross-species transmission(1). Mammalian hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, order 62 Elliovirales) are emerging zoonotic pathogens that cause severe, often fatal illness in 63 humans after transmission from chronically infected small-mammal reservoirs, 64 manifesting as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and 65 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (2, 3). The public health 66 significance of hantaviruses is underscored by their recurring emergence, including a 67 multi-country HCPS outbreak in April-May 2026, which involved limited secondary 68 transmission and resulted in three reported deaths (4–6). Despite significant morbidity 69 and high case-fatality rates approaching 40% for HCPS, no FDA-approved 70 prophylactics or antiviral therapeutics are currently available (7). Cellular entry of 71 hantaviruses is orchestrated entirely by the envelope glycoprotein complex Gn/Gc (8, 72 9). Gn and Gc are synthesized as a single polyprotein precursor encoded by the 73 medium (M) genomic segment, co-translationally cleaved by cellular signal peptidases, 74 and assemble into spike-like tetramers of Gn/Gc heterodimers on the virion envelope 75 (8–11)These glycoproteins coordinate entry: the membrane-distal Gn subunit likely 76 mediates host receptor engagement, while the class II fusion protein Gc drives low-pH- 77 dependent membrane fusion within late endosomes envelope (8–12) Despite the 78 identification of dozens of hantavirus species across rodent and insectivore hosts 79 globally, host entry receptors and neutralization vulnerabilities for most divergent 80 species remain undefined (10, 13, 14). 81 Candidate hantavirus attachment factors and receptors initially identified through 82 antibody blockade, ligand competition, or in vitro binding assays include β1, β2, and β3 83 integrins, decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55), and gC1qR complement receptor (15– 84 19). However, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function screens in human 85 microvascular endothelial cells, a primary in vivo target cell type, demonstrated that 86 knockout of ITGB1, ITGB3, or DAF had little or no effect on infection by a panel of 87 virulent hantaviruses, indicating that these molecules are dispensable for endothelial 88 cell entry (20). Unbiased haploid-genetic screening instead identified protocadherin-1 89 (PCDH1) as an essential entry receptor for Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus 90 andesense) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense): its 91 membrane-distal extracellular cadherin domain 1 (EC1) directly binds Gn/Gc, and 92 genetic ablation of PCDH1 in cultured cells and Syrian hamsters protects against ANDV 93 infection and lethal disease (21). Point mutations within the EC1 contact surface disrupt 94 infection, establishing PCDH1-EC1 as the functional interface (22). Although PCDH1 95 usage has been established for multiple hantaviruses, the glycoprotein determinants 96 that govern receptor recognition across divergent lineages remain incompletely defined 97 (20–22). PCDH1 usage has also been documented beyond the canonical New World 98 clade, including in vole- and mole-borne viruses (23), but its distribution across other 99 rodent- and shrew-borne clades has yet to be fully mapped. 100 Gn/Gc amino acid sequences differ by roughly 40-60% between hantavirus lineages, 101 and most glycoprotein-directed monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) raised or isolated against 102 one species show little heterologous neutralization (24, 25). Consequently, broadly 103 active entry inhibitors may need to target either conserved virus-receptor interfaces or 104 rare, functionally constrained epitopes on the viral spike (11, 21, 24, 25). On the host 105 side, the EC1-specific mAb-3305, soluble histidine-tagged PCDH1 ectodomain proteins 106 containing EC1-2 or EC1-4 (sEC1-2, sEC1-4), and a human Fc-tagged soluble EC1 107 decoy (EC1-Fc) block PCDH1-Gn/Gc engagement and neutralize PCDH1-dependent 108 viruses (21–23). Conversely, targeting conserved epitopes on the viral spike can 109 provide broad neutralization across clades. In particular, mAb-42898, isolated from a 110 Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus puumalaense)-convalescent individual, binds a 111 quaternary epitope bridging the Gn capping loop and Gc fusion loops, neutralizes 112 multiple HCPS- and HFRS-causing viruses, and protects rodents against lethal 113 challenge (24, 26). Evaluating an expanded panel of uncharacterized Gn/Gc complexes 114 against both receptor-targeted and spike-targeted approaches can reveal conserved 115 viral vulnerabilities and inform the development of broadly active therapeutics. 116 Functional entry studies of less-characterized hantaviruses are constrained by the 117 limited availability of cultivable isolates and the requirement for biosafety level 3 or 4 118 (BSL3/4) containment for pathogenic hantaviruses (10). Here, we generated replication- 119 competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) expressing an enhanced 120 green fluorescent protein (eGFP) reporter and bearing codon-optimized Gn/Gc 121 complexes from six ecologically and phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses: the HCPS- 122 associated Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV, Orthohantavirus nigrorivense; carried by 123 Hispid cotton rat) (27) and Laguna Negra virus (LANV, Orthohantavirus mamorense; 124 small vesper mouse) (28); the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus (DBSV, 125 Orthohantavirus dabieshanense; Chinese white-bellied rat) (29) and Tigray virus (TIGV, 126 Orthohantavirus tigrayense; Ethiopian white-footed mouse) (30, 31); the shrew-borne 127 Cao Bang virus (CBNV, Orthohantavirus caobangense; Chinese mole shrew) (32) and 128 Amga virus (MGAV, Orthohantavirus artybashense; Laxmann's shrew) (33, 34). This 129 panel includes viruses with distinct and incompletely defined zoonotic relevance. TIGV 130 circulates in peridomestic rodents in Ethiopia, where orthohantavirus-reactive antibodies 131 were detected in human sera (35). DBSV is genetically related to the prototypic HFRS- 132 causing Hantaan virus (HTNV), whereas CBNV and MGAV are shrew-borne viruses 133 with no established association with human disease (13, 29). 134 BCCV and LANV are particularly notable because authentic isolates exist for both, and 135 each has been studied extensively in epidemiologic, reservoir, and animal-model 136 settings. BCCV persists asymptomatically with horizontal transmission in its natural 137 reservoir but is uniformly lethal in immunosuppressed Syrian hamsters (36–38), 138 whereas LANV causes HCPS across South America and lethal pulmonary disease in 139 Turkish hamsters (39). Despite this substantial body of work, the receptor requirements 140 of both viruses remain undefined: BCCV entry was last examined before any hantavirus 141 receptor was identified (40) and neither virus has been tested for PCDH1 dependence. 142 To recover replication-competent rVSVs bearing Old World rodent-borne and shrew- 143 borne glycoproteins, we engineered Gn/Gc constructs using previously established 144 HTNV-based rescue-enhancing substitutions (23, 41). Here we show that all six Gn/Gc 145 complexes mediate infection of human microvascular endothelial cells, consistent with 146 systematic pseudotype screens showing that receptor-binding proteins from diverse 147 animal viruses can function broadly in human cells (1). CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic 148 depletion and cDNA complementation in human cells demonstrated that infection 149 mediated by glycoproteins of BCCV and LANV—but not those of DBSV, TIGV, CBNV, 150 or MGAV—depends on PCDH1. Concordantly, BCCV and LANV glycoproteins bound 151 soluble PCDH1 with different efficiencies in sEC1-2 capture ELISAs, were competitively 152 blocked at this interface by EC1-specific mAb-3305, and were neutralized by EC1-Fc 153 and mAb-3305 in endothelial cell infection assays. Finally, ADI-42898 bound all six 154 Gn/Gc-bearing particles and neutralized them with variable potency that correlated with 155 naturally occurring amino acid variation at epitope sites corresponding to PUUV 156 residues Q98, E750, and E768. Together, our findings expand the known diversity of 157 hantavirus receptor usage and define human endothelial cell susceptibility and antibody 158 sensitivity profiles across an expanded spectrum of hantavirus glycoproteins. 159 Results 160 Gn/Gc complexes from divergent rodent- and shrew-borne hantaviruses mediate 161 infection of human endothelial cells 162 We evaluated whether Gn/Gc glycoproteins from six phylogenetically and ecologically 163 distinct hantaviruses could mediate infection of human endothelial cells. The panel 164 included the New World rodent-borne viruses Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV) and 165 Laguna Negra virus (LANV), the Old World rodent-borne viruses Dabieshan virus 166 (DBSV) and Tigray virus (TIGV), and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus (CBNV) and 167 Amga virus (MGAV) (Fig. 1A). Although cell culture isolates are available for BCCV and 168 LANV (27, 28), authenticated isolates have not been reported for DBSV, TIGV, CBNV 169 or MGAV, which are known from viral sequences recovered from reservoir tissues. 170 To examine Gn/Gc-mediated entry under BSL2 conditions, we generated replication- 171 competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) in which the native VSV G 172 open reading frame was replaced with the Gn/Gc open reading frame from LANV, 173 BCCV, DBSV, CBNV, TIGV, or MGAV. An enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) 174 reporter was included in the first transcriptional unit to permit quantitation of infected 175 cells (Fig. 1B, top). Consistent with established rVSV rescue strategies for Old World 176 rodent-borne, mole-, and shrew-borne viruses, constructs from DBSV, CBNV, TIGV, 177 and MGAV contained the Hantaan virus (HTNV)-derived rescue-enhancing substitutions 178 I532K in the Gn cytoplasmic tail and S1094L in the membrane-proximal stem of Gc 179 ectodomain (23, 41) (Fig. 1B bottom). In selected constructs, adjacent residues were 180 also replaced with their HTNV counterparts. These modifications promote plasma- 181 membrane localization and rVSV incorporation of HTNV Gn/Gc and lie outside the 182 receptor-binding interface and the mapped neutralizing-antibody epitopes evaluated 183 here. 184 Recovery of rVSV-BCCV required an S430C substitution. Because cysteine is highly 185 conserved at the corresponding position among mammalian hantaviruses, the serine 186 reported in the deposited BCCV GenBank sequence may reflect a sequencing error 187 rather than authentic viral variation. Nanopore sequencing of rescued rVSV stocks 188 identified no additional nonsynonymous changes beyond the engineered substitutions, 189 except for G485R in rVSV-MGAV. This substitution has also been observed during 190 rescue of rVSV bearing the related Kenkeme virus Gn/Gc (23) but not for most other 191 hantavirus Gn/Gc proteins (20, 21, 42–44). G485, the terminal residue of the Gn 192 ectodomain, is highly conserved among hantaviruses; however, the functional 193 consequences of the G485R substitution remain unknown. 194 We then measured infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial 195 cells (HPMECs) over 48 h at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 (Fig. 1C and D). Virus 196 inputs were normalized using titers determined in permissive Huh-7.5.1 cells. At 12 h 197 postinfection (hpi), rVSV-LANV and rVSV-DBSV infection approached or exceeded that 198 of the rVSV-ANDV control, with approximately 30-40% of cells becoming eGFP positive 199 (Fig. 1C and D). Infection by these viruses and by rVSV-ANDV peaked between 24 and 200 36 hpi, reaching approximately 70-90% eGFP positive cells (Fig. 1D). In contrast, rVSV- 201 BCCV infection was only minimally detectable at 12 hpi, at approximately 4%, and 202 increased to a plateau of approximately 20% by 24 hpi (Fig. 1D). rVSV-CBNV, rVSV- 203 TIGV, and rVSV-MGAV produced slower and lower-level infection, becoming readily 204 detectable only at 48 hpi, when approximately 4-8% of cells were eGFP positive (Fig. 205 1C and D). 206 Thus, all six Gn/Gc complexes mediated infection of primary human endothelial cells 207 but differed substantially in infection efficiency and kinetics. These data establish human 208 endothelial-cell entry competence for LANV and BCCV Gn/Gc and provide functional 209 evidence that the Gn/Gc complexes of DBSV, TIGV, CBNV, and MGAV can mediate 210 cellular entry. 211 BCCV and LANV Gn/Gc-mediated infection depends on PCDH1 212 We next tested whether the Gn/Gc complexes in this panel require PCDH1 for entry. 213 Wild-type (WT), PCDH1-knockout cells transduced with empty vector (KO + EV), and 214 PCDH1-knockout cells complemented with PCDH1 cDNA (KO + PCDH1) were infected 215 with the indicated rVSVs. These genetic backgrounds in previously validated human 216 osteosarcoma U2OS and telomerase-immortalized human microvascular endothelial 217 (TIME) cell systems enable distinction between PCDH1-dependent and PCDH1- 218 independent hantavirus entry pathways (20–23). 219 In U2OS cells, PCDH1 ablation reduced infection by rVSV-BCCV and rVSV-LANV by 220 approximately 50-60%, similar to the reduction observed for the PCDH1-dependent 221 rVSV-ANDV control (Fig. 2A). PCDH1 re-expression restored rVSV-LANV and rVSV- 222 ANDV infection. Infection by rVSV-BCCV also increased after PCDH1 223 complementation, reaching levels above those observed in WT cells. In contrast, 224 PCDH1 status had little or no effect on infection by rVSV-DBSV, rVSV-CBNV, rVSV- 225 TIGV, and rVSV-MGAV, paralleling the well-established PCDH1-independent infection 226 of rVSV-HTNV. 227 We confirmed this phenotype in TIME cells, providing an endothelial cell context 228 relevant to hantavirus tropism. In these cells, PCDH1 knockout reduced rVSV-BCCV 229 and rVSV-LANV infection by approximately 75% relative to WT cells, comparable to the 230 reduction observed for rVSV-ANDV (Fig. 2B). rVSV-HTNV infection was not 231 significantly affected by PCDH1 knockout. Jangra1,* 4 5 1 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Center for Applied Immunology and 6 Pathological Processes, Center for Cardiovascular Diseases and Sciences, Louisiana 7 State University Health Sciences Center-Shreveport, Shreveport, Louisiana, USA. 8 2 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, 9 Bronx, New York, USA. 10 11 † Current address: Norgen Biotek, Thorold, Ontario, Canada. 12 ‡ Current address: Fundacion Instituto Leloir, Buenos Aires, Argentina. 13 14 * Corresponding author: Rohit K Jangra (rohit.jangra@lsuhs.edu) 15 16 17 Word counts: 18 19 Abstract: 242 20 Importance: 129 21 22 Abstract 23 Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with 24 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have 25 not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis 26 viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by 27 these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the 28 shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported 29 infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific 30 efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection 31 mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human 32 osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored 33 susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the 34 first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy 35 containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, 36 indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black 37 Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower 38 apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing 39 particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 40 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc 41 complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for 42 efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1- 43 directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly 44 reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. 45 Importance 46 The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely 47 characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we 48 show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses 49 associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for 50 efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two 51 viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that 52 PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes 53 from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents 54 infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, 55 emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody 56 neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein 57 surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown. 58 59 Introduction 60 Entry of enveloped viruses into host cells is a major determinant of tissue tropism and 61 cross-species transmission(1). Mammalian hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, order 62 Elliovirales) are emerging zoonotic pathogens that cause severe, often fatal illness in 63 humans after transmission from chronically infected small-mammal reservoirs, 64 manifesting as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and 65 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (2, 3). The public health 66 significance of hantaviruses is underscored by their recurring emergence, including a 67 multi-country HCPS outbreak in April-May 2026, which involved limited secondary 68 transmission and resulted in three reported deaths (4–6). Despite significant morbidity 69 and high case-fatality rates approaching 40% for HCPS, no FDA-approved 70 prophylactics or antiviral therapeutics are currently available (7). Cellular entry of 71 hantaviruses is orchestrated entirely by the envelope glycoprotein complex Gn/Gc (8, 72 9). Gn and Gc are synthesized as a single polyprotein precursor encoded by the 73 medium (M) genomic segment, co-translationally cleaved by cellular signal peptidases, 74 and assemble into spike-like tetramers of Gn/Gc heterodimers on the virion envelope 75 (8–11)These glycoproteins coordinate entry: the membrane-distal Gn subunit likely 76 mediates host receptor engagement, while the class II fusion protein Gc drives low-pH- 77 dependent membrane fusion within late endosomes envelope (8–12) Despite the 78 identification of dozens of hantavirus species across rodent and insectivore hosts 79 globally, host entry receptors and neutralization vulnerabilities for most divergent 80 species remain undefined (10, 13, 14). 81 Candidate hantavirus attachment factors and receptors initially identified through 82 antibody blockade, ligand competition, or in vitro binding assays include β1, β2, and β3 83 integrins, decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55), and gC1qR complement receptor (15– 84 19). However, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function screens in human 85 microvascular endothelial cells, a primary in vivo target cell type, demonstrated that 86 knockout of ITGB1, ITGB3, or DAF had little or no effect on infection by a panel of 87 virulent hantaviruses, indicating that these molecules are dispensable for endothelial 88 cell entry (20). Unbiased haploid-genetic screening instead identified protocadherin-1 89 (PCDH1) as an essential entry receptor for Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus 90 andesense) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense): its 91 membrane-distal extracellular cadherin domain 1 (EC1) directly binds Gn/Gc, and 92 genetic ablation of PCDH1 in cultured cells and Syrian hamsters protects against ANDV 93 infection and lethal disease (21). Point mutations within the EC1 contact surface disrupt 94 infection, establishing PCDH1-EC1 as the functional interface (22). Although PCDH1 95 usage has been established for multiple hantaviruses, the glycoprotein determinants 96 that govern receptor recognition across divergent lineages remain incompletely defined 97 (20–22). PCDH1 usage has also been documented beyond the canonical New World 98 clade, including in vole- and mole-borne viruses (23), but its distribution across other 99 rodent- and shrew-borne clades has yet to be fully mapped. 100 Gn/Gc amino acid sequences differ by roughly 40-60% between hantavirus lineages, 101 and most glycoprotein-directed monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) raised or isolated against 102 one species show little heterologous neutralization (24, 25). Consequently, broadly 103 active entry inhibitors may need to target either conserved virus-receptor interfaces or 104 rare, functionally constrained epitopes on the viral spike (11, 21, 24, 25). On the host 105 side, the EC1-specific mAb-3305, soluble histidine-tagged PCDH1 ectodomain proteins 106 containing EC1-2 or EC1-4 (sEC1-2, sEC1-4), and a human Fc-tagged soluble EC1 107 decoy (EC1-Fc) block PCDH1-Gn/Gc engagement and neutralize PCDH1-dependent 108 viruses (21–23). analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and their cellular entry receptors are largely unknown.
analysis.methods: Replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes of six hantaviruses were used to infect primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells; PCDH1 was genetically ablated or re‑expressed in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells; soluble PCDH1 ectodomains and domain‑specific antibodies were used to capture or inhibit virus entry.
analysis.results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected endothelial cells; PCDH1 loss reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, while re‑expression restored susceptibility; soluble PCDH1 and a first‑cadherin‑domain decoy inhibited entry, indicating EC1 mediates engagement; Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc incorporated less protein and showed lower capture and inhibitor sensitivity; the other four hantaviruses were unaffected by PCDH1 depletion; all viruses were potently neutralized by the broadly reactive antibody ADI‑42898.
analysis.contribution: The study shows that Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, underscoring heterogeneity even among closely related viruses; it also identifies a broadly neutralizing antibody that targets conserved glycoprotein surfaces, offering a therapeutic avenue when receptor usage is diverse.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HCPS and their cellular entry receptors are largely unknown. Methods: rVSVs bearing Gn/Gc of six hantaviruses infected primary human endothelial cells; PCDH1 was knocked out or re‑expressed; soluble PCDH1 and domain‑specific antibodies were used for capture and inhibition. Results: All six viruses infected cells; PCDH1 loss reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, while re‑expression restored it; soluble PCDH1 and a first‑cadherin‑domain decoy blocked entry, indicating EC1 mediates engagement; Black Creek Canal had lower capture and inhibitor sensitivity; the other four viruses were unaffected by PCDH1 depletion; all were neutralized by ADI‑42898. Contribution: Demonstrates PCDH1 is essential for entry of Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses but usage varies, highlighting the need for alternative receptors for other hantaviruses and a broadly neutralizing antibody as a therapeutic target. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Vaccines for the prevention of hantavirus fevers: An overview of results and development prospects
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION. Hantavirus fevers, known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with a wide range of clinical manifestations. The causative agents are members of the genus Orthohantavirus , whose natural reservoirs are rodents of various species. There is currently no etiotropic therapy for these diseases. Specific prophylaxis through vaccination is available only in the DPRK, the Republic of Korea, and the People's Republic of China. An important objective is to provide the Russian and European markets with a relevant vaccine for HFRS prevention. Such a vaccine should be developed based on both time-proven approaches and the experience of modern developments. AIM. Analysis of the use of existing hantavirus vaccines and the specific features of vaccines under development, as well as assessment of the prospects for creating vaccines for HFRS prevention in the Russian Federation. DISCUSSION. All commercially available vaccine preparations are inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on the Hantaan and Seoul viruses. The effectiveness of these preparations varies, but a significant reduction in the incidence rate in regions with mass vaccination and a low incidence of adverse events have been noted. Several inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on relevant orthohantavirus strains have been developed in Russia. Some of these developments have successfully completed preclinical studies. The spectrum of hantavirus vaccine preparations under development includes subunit vaccines, vaccines based on virus-like particles (VLPs) and viral vectors, DNA vaccines, and mRNA vaccines. The primary immunogens are the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc of hantaviruses. The closest to implementation into clinical practice are the DNA vaccines based on the Puumala and Hantaan viruses, which have undergone clinical trials (phase I). CONCLUSIONS. No vaccine for the prevention of hantavirus infections developed using virus-like particles (VLPs), viral vectors, or nucleic acids (DNA or mRNA) has undergone a full cycle of clinical trials or been licensed worldwide. On the contrary, well-established traditional technologies for manufacturing inactivated vaccines and their time-proven effectiveness provide a basis for their real prospects of practical application in the Russian Federation and other European countries.

The closest to implementation into clinical practice are the DNA vaccines based on the Puumala and Hantaan viruses, which have undergone clinical trials (phase I). CONCLUSIONS. No vaccine for the prevention of hantavirus infections developed using virus-like particles (VLPs), viral vectors, or nucleic acids (DNA or mRNA) has undergone a full cycle of clinical trials or been licensed worldwide. On the contrary, well-established traditional technologies for manufacturing inactivated vaccines and their time-proven effectiveness provide a basis for their real prospects of practical application in the Russian Federation and other European countries.

papers.full_text: Вакцины для профилактики хантавирусных лихорадок: обзор результатов и перспектив разработок https://doi.org/10.30895/2221-996X-2026-26-3-324-335 Резюме ВВЕДЕНИЕ. Хантавирусные лихорадки, регистрируемые как геморрагическая лихорадка с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) на Евроазиатском и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС) на Американском континентах, представляют собой природно-очаговые болезни с широким диапазоном клинических проявлений. Возбудители — представители рода Orthohantavirus, резервуаром которых в природе являются грызуны различных видов. Этиотропной терапии хантавирусных лихорадок в настоящее время не существует. Специфическая профилактика в форме вакцинации проводится только в КНДР, Республике Корее и КНР. Важной задачей является обеспечение российского и европейского рынка актуальной вакциной для профилактики ГЛПС. Противохантавирусная вакцина должна разрабатываться как с учетом подходов, доказавших временем свою эффективность, так и опыта современных разработок. ЦЕЛЬ. Анализ применения существующих хантавирусных и особенностей разрабатываемых вакцин, а также оценка перспектив создания вакцин для профилактики ГЛПС в Российской Федерации. ОБСУЖДЕНИЕ. Все коммерчески доступные вакцинные препараты являются инактивированными цельновирионными вакцинами на основе вирусов Хантаан и Сеул. Эффективность этих препаратов различается, но отмечается существенное снижение заболеваемости в регионах с массовой вакцинацией и низкая частота побочных явлений. В России разработаны несколько инактивированных цельновирионных вакцин на основе актуальных штаммов ортохантавирусов. Некоторые из разработок успешно прошли доклинические испытания. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. analysis.background: Hantavirus fevers, known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with a wide range of clinical manifestations.
analysis.methods: The paper is a narrative overview; no primary study design, sample collection, or experimental methods are reported.
analysis.results: All commercially available vaccines are inactivated whole‑virion preparations (Hantaan, Seoul) that have lowered incidence in mass‑vaccination regions with few adverse events; Russia has developed several inactivated vaccines, some of which have passed preclinical studies; the development pipeline includes subunit, VLP, viral‑vector, DNA and mRNA vaccines, with DNA vaccines based on Puumala and Hantaan reaching phase I trials, while VLP, vector and nucleic‑acid vaccines have not completed full clinical cycles.
analysis.contribution: The review emphasizes the need for a Russian and European HFRS vaccine and argues that traditional inactivated vaccine technologies offer realistic prospects for implementation, informing future vaccine development and public‑health planning.
analysis.limitations: The article provides only a descriptive overview without original efficacy data, detailed clinical trial results, or comprehensive methodological information; evidence is limited to abstract and partial text.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus fevers (HFRS, HPS) are natural focal diseases with diverse clinical manifestations. Methods: This is a narrative overview; no primary study design or experimental methods are reported. Results: Existing inactivated whole‑virion vaccines (Hantaan, Seoul) reduce incidence where mass‑vaccinated and have low adverse events; Russia has several inactivated vaccines, some completing preclinical work, and is pursuing subunit, VLP, viral‑vector, DNA and mRNA platforms, with DNA vaccines (Puumala, Hantaan) reaching phase I, while VLP, vector and nucleic‑acid vaccines have not completed full trials. Contribution: The review highlights the need for a Russian/European HFRS vaccine and suggests traditional inactivated vaccines have realistic implementation prospects, guiding development and policy. Limitations: Only a descriptive overview is provided, lacking original efficacy data or detailed trial results; evidence is limited to abstract and partial text.

papers.title_zh: 用于预防汉坦病毒热的疫苗:结果概述与发展前景

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 发热,在欧亚地区称为 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),在美洲称为 汉坦病毒肺综合征(HPS),是自然灶性疾病,临床表现范围广泛。
analysis_zh.methods: 本文为叙述性综述;未报告任何原始研究设计、样本采集或实验方法。
analysis_zh.results: 所有商业可用的疫苗均为灭活全病毒制剂(汉滩病毒、首尔病毒),在大规模接种地区降低了发病率,且不良事件较少;俄罗斯已研发多种灭活疫苗,其中部分已通过临床前研究;研发管线包括亚单位、病毒样颗粒、病毒载体、DNA和mRNA疫苗,其中基于普马拉病毒和汉滩病毒的DNA疫苗已进入I期临床试验,而病毒样颗粒、载体和核酸疫苗尚未完成完整的临床周期。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述强调俄罗斯和欧洲亟需肾综合征出血热疫苗,并指出传统的灭活疫苗技术具备切实可行的实施前景,为未来疫苗研发和公共卫生规划提供参考。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本文仅提供描述性概述,缺乏原始疗效数据、详细临床试验结果或完整的方法学信息;证据仅限于摘要和部分正文。

papers.title: Climate change as an amplifier of hantavirus risk in South Asia: a neglected nexus.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is seroepidemiologically established in South Asian human populations and rodent reservoirs, with anti-hantavirus antibodies confirmed in occupational risk groups in India, an independent association with chronic kidney disease demonstrated in Sri Lanka, and co-infection with leptospirosis identified in more than one-fifth of hospitalized leptospirosis patients. Despite this, the intersection of these findings with the region's intensifying monsoon floods, rapid urbanization, and climate-driven rodent ecology remains entirely unexamined. This letter highlights the neglected climate-hantavirus nexus, identifies structural vulnerabilities that amplify transmission risk in South Asia, and calls for integrated flood-response surveillance and One Health coordination across the region.
papers.journal: Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

papers.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

source_records.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

papers.full_text: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning Abstract Seoul virus is an important rodent-borne hantavirus that can cause serious illness in humans, while Streptococcus pyogenes is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen associated with a wide range of infections and severe complications. The interaction between these two infections is not well understood from a mathematical modeling perspective. In this work, we develop a fractal–fractional model to investigate the transmission and co-infection dynamics of Seoul virus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The model is described using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo fractal–fractional derivative so that the effects of memory and the nonuniform nature of disease transmission can be represented more realistically than in conventional integer-order models. Several mathematical properties of the proposed system are studied, including the existence and uniqueness of solutions and the behavior of the disease-free equilibrium. The basic reproduction number is obtained to identify the threshold conditions associated with the spread of the infections, and the Ulam–Hyers stability of the model is also examined. In addition to the theoretical analysis, a physics-informed neural network is constructed to approximate the solutions of the fractal–fractional system. The governing equations and initial conditions are incorporated into the neural-network training process, allowing the model structure to guide the numerical approximation. The simulations illustrate the influence of the fractional and fractal parameters on the evolution of the co-infection system and show that the PINN approach can reproduce the model dynamics with good accuracy. The findings suggest that combining fractal–fractional operators with physics-informed learning offers a useful way to study co-infectious disease systems in which memory, heterogeneity, and nonlinear interactions play an important role. analysis.background: Seoul virus is an important rodent‑borne hantavirus that can cause serious illness in humans, and Streptococcus pyogenes is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen; the interaction between these two infections is not well understood from a mathematical modeling perspective.
analysis.methods: A fractal‑fractional model was developed using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative to capture memory and non‑uniform transmission; the basic reproduction number and Ulam–Hyers stability were derived; a physics‑informed neural network incorporating the governing equations and initial conditions was constructed to approximate solutions.
analysis.results: Mathematical analysis demonstrated existence and uniqueness of solutions and characterized the disease‑free equilibrium; the reproduction number identified threshold conditions for spread; simulations showed that fractional and fractal parameters influence co‑infection dynamics and that the PINN reproduces model behavior with good accuracy.
analysis.contribution: The study shows that combining fractal‑fractional operators with physics‑informed learning offers a novel framework for investigating co‑infectious disease systems where memory, heterogeneity, and nonlinear interactions are important.
analysis.limitations: No empirical validation, quantitative results, or detailed methodological data are reported; the evidence consists only of abstract and partial text, so full limitations are not provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Seoul virus is a serious rodent‑borne hantavirus and Streptococcus pyogenes a major bacterial pathogen, yet their interaction is poorly understood mathematically. Methods: A fractal‑fractional model using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative was built, basic reproduction number and Ulam–Hyers stability were derived, and a physics‑informed neural network incorporated the equations for numerical approximation. Results: The model has unique solutions, a characterized disease‑free equilibrium, threshold conditions from the reproduction number, and simulations show parameter effects and accurate PINN reproduction. Contribution: This demonstrates a novel fractal‑fractional and physics‑informed approach for studying memory‑dependent co‑infection dynamics. Limitations: No empirical data or detailed results are provided; only abstract and partial text are available.

papers.title: Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome

source_records.title: Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome

papers.full_text: 245 EDITORIAL Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome Hantavirus: de Seúl a los Andes — La necesidad imperativa de incluirlo en el triaje del síndrome febril agudo Salim Mattar1,*, Vaneza Tique-Salleg2, Juan Carlos Sepúlveda-Arias3, Camilo Guzmán-Terán4 1 Universidad de Córdoba, Instituto de Investigaciones Biológicas del Trópico, Monteria Córdoba, Colombia. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0526-4630 2 Universidad de Córdoba, Instituto de Investigaciones Biológicas del Trópico, Monteria Córdoba, Colombia. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2629-6685 3 Grupo Infección e Inmunidad, Facultad de Ciencias de la Salud, Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira, Pereira 660003, Colombia. Editor-in-Chief, Infectio. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5410-5997 4 Universidad de Córdoba, Facultad Ciencias de la Salud, Departamen- to de Regencia en Farmacia, Monteria Córdoba, Colombia. https://orcid. org/0000-0001-5616-1071 Recibido: 25/08/2026; Aceptado: 25/08/2026 Cómo citar este artículo: S. Mattar, et al. Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome. Infectio 2026; 30(3): 245-246 Keywords: Hantavirus, Acute Febrile Syndrome, Rattus norvegicus Palabras clave: Hantavirus, Síndrome febril agudo, Rattus norvegicus Hantaviruses belong to two worlds: the Old-World Seoul vi- rus (SV) and New World hantaviruses, such as the Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in North America and Andes virus in South Ameri- ca. SV is a cosmopolitan hantavirus that is transmitted by the common brown rat (Rattus norvegicus). The virus lives in urban rodents and travels on ships. It causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which has low lethality. New World hantaviruses, such as SNV and Andes virus, cause Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), a condition with high lethality ranging between 30% and 40%. The transmission routes for both groups are similar, primarily occurring through contact with aerosolized rodent excretions and secretions1. The geography of zoonotic diseases is often marked by pro- found contrast. In the fabric of global health, few pathogens exemplify this as starkly as hantavirus. In the Old World, SV adapted to synanthropic rodents (Rattus rattus, Rattus nor- vegicus, and Mus musculus), which in turn adapted to urban environments enriched with human food waste. SV is trans- mitted in metropolitan settings with moderate lethality ra- tes, although it may be underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed as other conditions, such as leptospirosis, particularly in Latin America, where cases are rarely reported2. In contrast, the na- rrative of the New World SNV changes completely. * Autor para correspondencia: Correo electrónico: smattar@correo.unicordoba.edu.co; mattarsalim@gmail.com In the Americas, hantaviruses emerge from wild ecosystems with high virulence and present clinically as HCPS. The vec- tors of these viruses are wild sigmodontine rodents (Oligory- zomys, Proechimys, Peromyscus, and Calomys) that feed on crops and local flora. However, evidence has demonstrated that SNV can infect multiple rodent species within geogra- phic regions experiencing human cases. This suggests that several rodent species may act as reservoirs and potential vectors for the transmission of H. longicornis to humans. Re- servoirs identified by SNV include Peromyscus boylii, Tamias minimus, and Mus musculus. The latter is ubiquitous in hou- seholds worldwide and is a well-known vector of the lym- phocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and Leptospira (3). New World hantaviruses are widely distributed across North America and exhibit high diversity, including SNV, New York virus, and Black Creek Canal virus in the United States; Cho- clo virus in Panama; Maporal virus in Venezuela; Machupo virus in Bolivia; Laguna Negra virus in Paraguay; Sabiá virus in Brazil; and the recently prominent Andes virus (ANDV) in Argentina and Chile (Figure 1). Following the corridor of the formidable Andes mountain range, the virus moves steadily alongside its rodent hosts across the mountains, jungles, and valleys. ANDV has cha- llenged the classical virological paradigm that orthohanta- viruses are transmitted strictly via exposure to rodent secre- tions and excretions. ANDV possesses the unique capacity S. Mattar, et al 246 ASOCIACIÓN COLOMBIANA DE INFECTOLOGÍA REVISTA INFECTIO for interhuman airborne transmission, as documented during the M/V Hondius cruise ship outbreak in April 2026. A total of 13 confirmed cases and three fatalities were epidemio- logically linked to the vessel, forcing numerous passengers into mandatory quarantine across various countries. Never- theless, person-to-person transmission remains uncommon and is predominantly associated with household exposure, intimate contact, caregiving without adequate personal pro- tective equipment, and prolonged exposure to poorly venti- lated or overcrowded environments4,5. This epidemiological journey, spanning from the alleys of Seoul to the forested regions of South America, is not a ran- dom evolutionary artifact but rather a direct reflection of environmental boundaries repeatedly breached by human activity. Today, hantaviruses are no longer exotic rarities con- fined to the pages of tropical medicine textbooks. Accele- rating ecological degradation and expanding anthropogenic frontiers force host reservoirs out of mountain ranges and wild savannas into closer proximity to human populations. The evolving landscape of hantavirus infections poses a ma- jor diagnostic and therapeutic challenge for infectious disea- se specialists. The core challenge lies not merely in managing critical clinical outcomes but in establishing early clinical sus- picion. The eco-epidemiology of the disease demands the inclusion of hantavirus in diagnostic algorithms for acute undifferentiated febrile illness in emergency departments. Early symptoms overlap with numerous seasonal and tropical pathogens; thus, the differential diagnosis must encompass influenza, betacoronavirus infections, mycoplasmosis, Q fe- ver, leptospirosis, malaria, rickettsiosis, dengue, Zika, Chikun- gunya, Mayaro, and Oropouche5. Importantly, preceding the ANDV outbreak on the M/V Hon- dius in April 2026, the Ministry of Public Health of Argentina confirmed 12 hantavirus cases and two deaths in Salta Pro- vince between January and March. Most infections occurred in the Orán Department, involving 10 men and two women aged 20–50 years, while 50 additional suspected cases remai- ned under investigation across multiple departments6. Similarly, between February and July 2026, the Ministry of Health of Chile confirmed 41 hantavirus cases and 14 deaths (34% mortality rate). Cases were reported across 11 regions from Valparaíso to Aysén, with the highest incidence rates per 100,000 inhabitants recorded in Aysén (1.84), Los Ríos (0.96), and Ñuble (0.95). The causative agent was identified as ANDV, vectored by the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys lon- gicaudatus). In Venezuela, by late July 2026, three deaths pre- senting with symptoms compatible with HCPS were reported in Anzoátegui, alongside two unexplained deaths among phy- sicians in Barinas; these cases remain unconfirmed7. Hantavirus outbreaks in Argentina, Chile, and the M/V Hon- dius cruise ship in 2026 highlight the need to revise epide- miological perspectives and clinical approaches to acute un- differentiated febrile illness in Latin America. The cruise ship outbreak remains one of the most significant events invol- ving ANDV, the only known hantavirus capable of interhu- man transmission. The outbreak was officially declared over, with no active transmission detected8. This eco-epidemiological and clinical challenge requires the expansion of diagnostic algorithms. The primary danger of hantavirus lies in its chameleon-like presentation during the early stages. Following anthropogenic ecosystem disruption and subsequent reservoir exposure5, patients enter a prodro- mal phase that closely mimics common tropical infections or viral respiratory illnesses, such as COVID-19. During the first 3 to 5 days, symptoms manifest as an acute undifferentiated febrile syndrome characterized by sudden high fever (>39°C), severe myalgias (particularly involving the back and lower ex- tremities), headache, chills, diaphoresis, and gastrointestinal distress, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain1,2. Increased vascular permeability driven by endothelial dysfunction is the hallmark feature of HCPS, driven by ele- vated viral loads and dysregulated inflammatory mediators, such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-6, and interferon- gamma. During this critical window, hantavirus infection is frequently misdiagnosed as dengue, influenza, leptospirosis, or COVID-19. In the case of ANDV, the transition to full HCPS Figure 1. Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome 247 occurs abruptly within hours, triggering a cytokine storm that leads to massive capillary leakage, non-cardiogenic pulmo- nary edema, and cardiogenic shock with high mortality ra- tes2,4. In most instances, establishing a diagnosis once frank respiratory failure develops is too late. This manuscript highlights an urgent priority for emergency triage: hantavirus must not remain a late diagnosis of exclu- sion but rather an active consideration in the systematic eva- luation of acute febrile syndromes and atypical pneumonias. Clinical suspicion should not be restricted to unexplained respiratory failure. We formally propose the integration of hantavirus into differential diagnostic protocols for patients reporting exposure to rural or wild environments within the preceding 4 weeks1. In countries such as Colombia, where endemic zones remain poorly defined, clinicians must rely on subtle early laboratory clues. The combination of thrombo- cytopenia, hemoconcentration, and circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes) on peripheral blood smears provides a cost-effective triad of suspicion prior to the appearance of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiography1-5. When routine respiratory panels yield negative results in pa- tients with rapidly progressive pneumonia or in those pre- senting with febrile syndromes accompanied by early hema- tologic abnormalities, ordering IgM/IgG serology or RT-PCR for hantavirus should be protocolized9. IgM antibodies are detectable in nearly 100% of patients during the prodromal phase and persist for 2–3 months. Concurrently, IgG levels rise rapidly and appear to persist for years, although it re- mains uncertain whether these antibodies confer long-term neutralizing protection9. This rapid serological response at clinical onset makes ELISA the diagnostic tool of choice in emergency settings, outperforming RT-PCR in later stages, as the viral load declines rapidly after the first week of illness5. Furthermore, the unique capacity of ANDV for person-to- person transmission5 elevates early diagnosis from a clinical necessity to an urgent priority for hospital biosecurity and public health. Suspecting hantavirus infection at first contact in emergency departments is not an overreaction; it repre- sents the single opportunity to alter a potentially fatal course. In Colombia, the potential circulation of ANDV remains unk- nown, necessitating expanded seroprevalence and ecological reservoir research. Serologically, ANDV displays cross-reacti- vity with other New World hantaviruses, particularly SNV. We hypothesized that native Colombian hantaviruses may mani- fest with less aggressive clinical presentations than ANDV or SNV. This aligns with the findings of five patients diagnosed with IgM seroconversion in Córdoba and Meta10,11, presen- ting clinical features similar to those documented for Choclo virus in Panama12. To date, molecular detection in Colombia has been limited to a short genomic segment of the Neco- clí virus identified in wild rodents (Zygodontomys cherriei), although its human pathogenicity remains uncharacterized13. The geographic span of hantaviruses from North America to Patagonia underscores the fragility of ecological boundaries, which are dynamic interfaces that elevate global disease risk. Addressing this challenge requires a paradigm shift in clinical practices. Infectious disease and emergency medicine can no longer operate in isolation from environmental changes; the clinician’s diagnostic approach must be aligned with local te- rritorial ecology and epidemiology5,14. Systematically incorporating hantavirus into emergency tria- ge for acute febrile illness and atypical pneumonia is not an abstract taxonomical exercise but an essential clinical and public health imperative. In Colombia, substantial knowledge gaps remain regarding rodent-borne pathogens, particularly hantaviruses and Arenaviruses. Early clinical suspicion rema- ins the most effective tool in emergency medicine. Learning to recognize subtle epidemiological and hematological sig- nals in the early stages provides the only realistic window for intervention before fatal complications arise, a race against time in which early detection represents a major victory for preventive medicine. Editor-in-Chief, Infectio. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5410-5997 4 Universidad de Córdoba, Facultad Ciencias de la Salud, Departamen- to de Regencia en Farmacia, Monteria Córdoba, Colombia. https://orcid. org/0000-0001-5616-1071 Recibido: 25/08/2026; Aceptado: 25/08/2026 Cómo citar este artículo: S. Mattar, et al. Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome. Infectio 2026; 30(3): 245-246 Keywords: Hantavirus, Acute Febrile Syndrome, Rattus norvegicus Palabras clave: Hantavirus, Síndrome febril agudo, Rattus norvegicus Hantaviruses belong to two worlds: the Old-World Seoul vi- rus (SV) and New World hantaviruses, such as the Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in North America and Andes virus in South Ameri- ca. SV is a cosmopolitan hantavirus that is transmitted by the common brown rat (Rattus norvegicus). The virus lives in urban rodents and travels on ships. It causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which has low lethality. New World hantaviruses, such as SNV and Andes virus, cause Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), a condition with high lethality ranging between 30% and 40%. The transmission routes for both groups are similar, primarily occurring through contact with aerosolized rodent excretions and secretions1. The geography of zoonotic diseases is often marked by pro- found contrast. In the fabric of global health, few pathogens exemplify this as starkly as hantavirus. In the Old World, SV adapted to synanthropic rodents (Rattus rattus, Rattus nor- vegicus, and Mus musculus), which in turn adapted to urban environments enriched with human food waste. SV is trans- mitted in metropolitan settings with moderate lethality ra- tes, although it may be underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed as other conditions, such as leptospirosis, particularly in Latin America, where cases are rarely reported2. In contrast, the na- rrative of the New World SNV changes completely. * Autor para correspondencia: Correo electrónico: smattar@correo.unicordoba.edu.co; mattarsalim@gmail.com In the Americas, hantaviruses emerge from wild ecosystems with high virulence and present clinically as HCPS. The vec- tors of these viruses are wild sigmodontine rodents (Oligory- zomys, Proechimys, Peromyscus, and Calomys) that feed on crops and local flora. However, evidence has demonstrated that SNV can infect multiple rodent species within geogra- phic regions experiencing human cases. This suggests that several rodent species may act as reservoirs and potential vectors for the transmission of H. longicornis to humans. Re- servoirs identified by SNV include Peromyscus boylii, Tamias minimus, and Mus musculus. The latter is ubiquitous in hou- seholds worldwide and is a well-known vector of the lym- phocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and Leptospira (3). New World hantaviruses are widely distributed across North America and exhibit high diversity, including SNV, New York virus, and Black Creek Canal virus in the United States; Cho- clo virus in Panama; Maporal virus in Venezuela; Machupo virus in Bolivia; Laguna Negra virus in Paraguay; Sabiá virus in Brazil; and the recently prominent Andes virus (ANDV) in Argentina and Chile (Figure 1). Following the corridor of the formidable Andes mountain range, the virus moves steadily alongside its rodent hosts across the mountains, jungles, and valleys. ANDV has cha- llenged the classical virological paradigm that orthohanta- viruses are transmitted strictly via exposure to rodent secre- tions and excretions. ANDV possesses the unique capacity S. Mattar, et al 246 ASOCIACIÓN COLOMBIANA DE INFECTOLOGÍA REVISTA INFECTIO for interhuman airborne transmission, as documented during the M/V Hondius cruise ship outbreak in April 2026. A total of 13 confirmed cases and three fatalities were epidemio- logically linked to the vessel, forcing numerous passengers into mandatory quarantine across various countries. Never- theless, person-to-person transmission remains uncommon and is predominantly associated with household exposure, intimate contact, caregiving without adequate personal pro- tective equipment, and prolonged exposure to poorly venti- lated or overcrowded environments4,5. This epidemiological journey, spanning from the alleys of Seoul to the forested regions of South America, is not a ran- dom evolutionary artifact but rather a direct reflection of environmental boundaries repeatedly breached by human activity. Today, hantaviruses are no longer exotic rarities con- fined to the pages of tropical medicine textbooks. Accele- rating ecological degradation and expanding anthropogenic frontiers force host reservoirs out of mountain ranges and wild savannas into closer proximity to human populations. The evolving landscape of hantavirus infections poses a ma- jor diagnostic and therapeutic challenge for infectious disea- se specialists. The core challenge lies not merely in managing critical clinical outcomes but in establishing early clinical sus- picion. The eco-epidemiology of the disease demands the inclusion of hantavirus in diagnostic algorithms for acute undifferentiated febrile illness in emergency departments. Early symptoms overlap with numerous seasonal and tropical pathogens; thus, the differential diagnosis must encompass influenza, betacoronavirus infections, mycoplasmosis, Q fe- ver, leptospirosis, malaria, rickettsiosis, dengue, Zika, Chikun- gunya, Mayaro, and Oropouche5. Importantly, preceding the ANDV outbreak on the M/V Hon- dius in April 2026, the Ministry of Public Health of Argentina confirmed 12 hantavirus cases and two deaths in Salta Pro- vince between January and March. Most infections occurred in the Orán Department, involving 10 men and two women aged 20–50 years, while 50 additional suspected cases remai- ned under investigation across multiple departments6. Similarly, between February and July 2026, the Ministry of Health of Chile confirmed 41 hantavirus cases and 14 deaths (34% mortality rate). Cases were reported across 11 regions from Valparaíso to Aysén, with the highest incidence rates per 100,000 inhabitants recorded in Aysén (1.84), Los Ríos (0.96), and Ñuble (0.95). The causative agent was identified as ANDV, vectored by the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys lon- gicaudatus). In Venezuela, by late July 2026, three deaths pre- senting with symptoms compatible with HCPS were reported in Anzoátegui, alongside two unexplained deaths among phy- sicians in Barinas; these cases remain unconfirmed7. Hantavirus outbreaks in Argentina, Chile, and the M/V Hon- dius cruise ship in 2026 highlight the need to revise epide- miological perspectives and clinical approaches to acute un- differentiated febrile illness in Latin America. The cruise ship outbreak remains one of the most significant events invol- ving ANDV, the only known hantavirus capable of interhu- man transmission. The outbreak was officially declared over, with no active transmission detected8. This eco-epidemiological and clinical challenge requires the expansion of diagnostic algorithms. papers.title: Network-Guided Drug Repurposing for Hantaan Virus Infection in Endothelial Cells: Pathway Analysis, Target Identification, and Mechanistic ODE Simulations
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, which are together the cause of more than 200,000 human cases every year. However, no specific antiviral therapy is approved. Here, we develop a three-stage computational framework for systematic drug repurposing. Transcriptome-wide analysis of hantavirus-infected human endothelial cells showed a response dominated by interferon pathways. A STRING protein–protein interaction network and a composite network centrality score identified 15 hub genes, including ISG15, IRF1, CXCL10, STAT1, and DDX58. Druggability and literature analysis of these hubs provided 12 repurposing candidates across four priority tiers. An ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of type I interferon signalling then evaluated eight drug perturbations. Early IFN-β achieved the fastest viral clearance (3.5 days) with reduced CXCL10 output. Early JAK inhibition delayed clearance (4.9 days) and increased IRF1-driven CXCL10. Our simulation showed that IFN-β combined with an anti-CXCL10 monoclonal antibody produced the best balance between antiviral effect and CXCL10 output. A structural sensitivity analysis showed the antiviral predictions to hold under an alternative network topology, while the chemokine predictions depended on it. This computational pipeline prioritises candidate therapies and phase-specific combinations for preclinical hantavirus studies.

A STRING protein–protein interaction network and a composite network centrality score identified 15 hub genes, including ISG15, IRF1, CXCL10, STAT1, and DDX58. Druggability and literature analysis of these hubs provided 12 repurposing candidates across four priority tiers. An ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of type I interferon signalling then evaluated eight drug perturbations. Early IFN-β achieved the fastest viral clearance (3.5 days) with reduced CXCL10 output. Early JAK inhibition delayed clearance (4.9 days) and increased IRF1-driven CXCL10. Our simulation showed that IFN-β combined with an anti-CXCL10 monoclonal antibody produced the best balance between antiviral effect and CXCL10 output. A structural sensitivity analysis showed the antiviral predictions to hold under an alternative network topology, while the chemokine predictions depended on it. This computational pipeline prioritises candidate therapies and phase-specific combinations for preclinical hantavirus studies.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause >200,000 cases of severe disease annually and lack approved antivirals. Methods: A three‑stage computational pipeline combined transcriptomics of infected endothelial cells, STRING network centrality to find 15 hub genes, druggability screening of 12 candidates, and ODE modelling of IFN signalling for eight drug perturbations. Results: Early IFN‑β cleared virus fastest (3.5 days) with lower CXCL10; early JAK inhibition delayed clearance (4.9 days) and raised CXCL10; IFN‑β plus anti‑CXCL10 antibody gave optimal balance; antiviral predictions were robust, chemokine predictions depended on network topology. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, lacking detailed methods and validation.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 引起肾综合征出血热,汉坦病毒心肺综合征 亦如此,两者合计每年导致超过 200,000 例人类感染,且尚未获批特异性抗病毒疗法。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者开发了一个三阶段计算框架:对汉坦病毒感染的人类内皮细胞进行全转录组分析,利用STRING蛋白‐蛋白相互作用网络并结合复合中心性评分识别15个枢纽基因,进行药物可及性和文献筛选以提出12个再利用候选药物,并构建I型干扰素信号的常微分方程模型评估八种药物扰动。
analysis_zh.results: 模拟结果显示,早期IFN‐β可实现最快的病毒清除(3.5天),伴随CXCL10降低;早期JAK抑制延迟清除(4.9天)并导致CXCL10升高;IFN‐β与抗CXCL10单克隆抗体的联合使用提供了最佳的抗病毒‐趋化因子平衡;敏感性分析表明,抗病毒预测对网络拓扑具有鲁棒性,而趋化因子预测则不具备。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该流程优先筛选候选疗法及针对不同阶段的药物组合,用于临床前汉坦病毒研究。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、实验验证和完整数据。

papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: an emerging fatal zoonotic infection.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome is a potentially fatal respiratory zoonotic infection caused by New World hantaviruses, and it is acquired mostly via inhaling aerosolized excreta from infected rodents. Over the past 30 years, HCPS has expanded beyond its initial foci, and recent events suggest a potential for spread beyond traditionally endemic regions. The disease rapidly progresses from a vague prodrome to acute cardiopulmonary failure with a high fatality rate despite optimum supportive treatment. Pathophysiology involves endothelial failure, increased vascular permeability, acute thrombocytopenia and excessive immunological responses resulting in capillary leak syndrome and cardiogenic shock. It is still hard to clinically suspect early since the prodromal symptoms are vague and mirror common viral infections and respiratory disorders. Diagnostic confirmation needs serological testing or genetic approaches, which are typically unavailable in resource-limited endemic situations, leading to considerable diagnostic delays. Management is generally supportive, with early ICU admission, judicious hydration management, mechanical breathing and cardiopulmonary support including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory patients. The recent multi-country Andes virus epidemic on a cruise ship in May 2026 highlights the potential for fast worldwide transmission of HCPS outside of usual endemic settings. This review summarizes the current information on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic techniques, and treatment options for HCPS. We also highlight the pressing need for improved global surveillance, rapid point-of-care diagnostics, global awareness among health care workers, and ongoing development of preventive vaccines and effective antiviral therapies to address this significant public health threat.

analysis.main_directions: The review discusses endothelial failure and capillary leak as key pathophysiological mechanisms, supportive ICU care including ECMO, and the need for surveillance, rapid diagnostics, vaccines, and antivirals (A4).
analysis.current_state: HCPS progresses rapidly from nonspecific prodrome to acute cardiopulmonary failure with high mortality despite optimal supportive treatment (A3).
analysis.gaps: Early clinical suspicion is difficult because prodromal symptoms are vague and mimic common infections (A5).
analysis.future_research: Priorities include strengthening global surveillance, developing point‑of‑care tests, advancing vaccine candidates, and identifying effective antiviral therapies (A10).

papers.title: Hantavirus in Dentistry: Occupational Exposure Considerations and a Proposed Tiered Infection Prevention and Control Framework-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective The aim of this study is to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission and occupational exposure pathways relevant to dentistry, and to propose an evidence‐informed tiered infection prevention and control (IPC) framework that distinguishes established from theoretical risk. Material and Methods The initial narrative search covered database inception through May 15, 2026 in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and WHO/CDC/ECDC/OSHA sources, followed by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and public‐health guidance update through August 18, 2026. Approximately 1450 records were identified. After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full‐text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer‐reviewed publications and 11 gray‐literature or public‐health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected‐rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person‐to‐person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture‐based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental‐aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental‐specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient‐related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission‐based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol‐generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence‐informed, author‐derived, and unvalidated.

analysis.background: The review aims to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission pathways relevant to dentistry and to propose a tiered infection‑prevention framework (A1).
analysis.main_directions: It surveys literature on environmental rodent exposure, limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, and the absence of documented dental transmission (A2, A5‑A8).
analysis.current_state: Environmental rodent contamination is the established occupational route, ANDV can be present in oral/respiratory fluids, but dental‑aerosol transmission has not been demonstrated and no cases are reported (A5‑A8, A10).
analysis.gaps: The magnitude of dental‑specific risk remains unquantified, and the proposed tiered IPC framework is author‑derived and unvalidated (A9, A13).
analysis.future_research: Validation of the tiered IPC model, quantitative risk assessment for dental settings, and surveillance for possible ANDV transmission during aerosol‑generating procedures are needed (A13).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The review synthesizes hantavirus transmission evidence for dentistry and proposes a tiered IPC framework (A1). Main directions: It examines rodent‑borne exposure, limited ANDV person‑to‑person spread, and the lack of documented dental transmission (A2, A5‑A8). Current state: Rodent exposure is the established risk; ANDV RNA is found in oral fluids but dental aerosol transmission is unproven (A5‑A8, A10). Gaps: Dental‑specific risk is unquantified and the IPC tiers are unvalidated (A9, A13). Future research: Validate the IPC tiers, quantify dental risk, and conduct surveillance for aerosol‑mediated ANDV spread (A13).

analysis_zh.background: 本综述旨在综合与牙科相关的 汉坦病毒 传播途径的证据,并提出分层感染预防框架 (A1)。

papers.title: Open ecological, genomic and digital behavioural data resolve the 2026 MV Hondius Andes virus outbreak to the southern-Andean reservoir zone
papers.abstract: Abstract The 2026 Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulted in 11 confirmed cases and 3 deaths and raised questions regarding the origin of infection, with much media focus resting on a landfill in Tierra del Fuego. We evaluated competing exposure hypotheses by assembling open data on reservoir host occurrences, rodent serosurveys, and historical ANDV outbreaks along with the index case’s self-documented, publicly-posted citizen-science digital record of their movements. Historical outbreaks associated with human-to-human transmission were concentrated within a restricted region spanning southern Chile and adjacent western Argentina, coinciding with the distribution of the principal reservoir host, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus , and areas identified as elevated risk by multiple ecological and genetic models. The index case was documented within this transmission focus shortly before the putative exposure period. Together, our open data approach was able to rapidly locate initial exposure within the established ANDV transmission focus and develop scenarios to prioritise further epidemiological investigation.

papers.title_zh: 开放的生态、基因组和数字行为数据将2026年MV Hondius 安第斯病毒疫情定位至南安第斯储存区

analysis_zh.background: 2026 年 安第斯病毒 在 MV Hondius 邮轮上的暴发导致 11 例确诊病例和 3 例死亡,引发对感染来源的疑问,媒体关注位于火地岛的垃圾填埋场。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究汇集了关于储存宿主(Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)分布、啮齿动物血清调查、历史 ANDV 暴发以及指数病例自行记录的数字移动轨迹的开放数据,以评估竞争性的暴露假设。
analysis_zh.results: 历史的人际传播集群局限于智利南部及相邻的阿根廷西部,覆盖宿主分布并与生态和遗传模型确定的高风险区域重叠;指数病例在假定暴露期前不久被记录在该传播焦点内。
analysis_zh.contribution: 开放数据方法快速定位了可能的暴露区,位于已确定的 ANDV 传播焦点内,并生成情景以优先开展进一步的流行病学调查。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、样本量、定量结果及更广泛的背景信息。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a persistent zoonotic risk: epidemiology and current pharmacological management.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that continue to pose a public health concern despite their relatively low incidence in humans. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship renewed international attention on these pathogens, highlighting unresolved questions regarding transmission dynamics, vulnerable populations, and global preparedness. This review provides an updated critical appraisal of recent advances in hantavirus epidemiology, emerging therapeutic strategies, and public health challenges, with particular emphasis on the 2026 Andes virus outbreak, companion animals, and solid organ transplant recipients. METHODS: A review of the recent literature was performed, focusing on zoonotic transmission, the role of companion animals, current and emerging therapeutic strategies, infections in immunocompromised and solid-organ transplant recipients, and the implications of the 2026 international outbreak. RESULTS: Although the sentinel hypothesis remains plausible, companion animals are not natural reservoirs, and preliminary evidence suggests that their exposure may reflect local hantavirus circulation, while pet rats have emerged as an important source of Seoul orthohantavirus infection. Therapeutic options remain limited: supportive care is the standard of treatment, and ribavirin shows benefit only in early hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. Emerging immunotherapeutic approaches, including neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and host-directed therapies, show promising preclinical results but still lack robust clinical validation. In immunocompromised patients, particularly solid-organ transplant recipients, hantavirus infection may mimic graft rejection or present with atypical, potentially fatal manifestations, posing diagnostic challenges. The 2026 MV Hondius outbreak reinforced the need for heightened surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and coordinated international response, while confirming that sustained human-to-human transmission remains exceptional. CONCLUSION: Recent evidence broadens the clinical and public health relevance of hantaviruses beyond their traditional framing as rodent-borne zoonoses. Advances in targeted therapeutics, integrated surveillance, and One Health preparedness will be pivotal to improving outbreak preparedness and accelerating the development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Climate change, rodent ecology, and the rising risk of hantavirus outbreaks: an alarming public health concern.
papers.abstract: The Anthropocene era has been characterized by a higher risk of zoonotic viral outbreaks, which often result from a combination of factors, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use patterns, and increased opportunities for human-animal interactions. The current perspective provides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, with an emphasis on the underlying virological mechanisms and their implications for One Health preparedness. Hantaviruses have undergone extensive diversification throughout their evolution and host adaptation and can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish. Rodents serve as the principal natural reservoirs for hantaviruses, with many viral species exhibiting long-term evolutionary associations with specific rodent host species. Climate change has been recognized as one of the key determinants for the emergence of hantavirus outbreaks in different parts of the world. Climate-related factors may facilitate viral amplification through multiple mechanisms, including their impact on evolution, mutation, and reassortment. To conclude, climate change has shaped the ecology, transmission dynamics, and molecular evolution of hantaviruses by altering rodent behavior, their habitats, and the environmental persistence of viral particles. Climate-induced ecological disruption has created opportunities for viral amplification within reservoir hosts and augmented the risk of zoonotic spillover into humans. These insights provide a conceptual framework for anticipating future outbreaks in the context of climate change and support the integration of ecological, virological, and public health surveillance systems. There is an urgent need to ensure that virological preparedness strategies evolve in accordance with changing environmental conditions by strengthening genomic surveillance and integrated One Health frameworks.

analysis_zh.background: 人类世时代因气候变化、生物多样性丧失、土地利用变化以及人畜接触增加,使人畜共患病毒暴发风险升高。(A1)
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该视角整合了气候驱动的啮齿动物生态变化对 汉坦病毒 分子进化、传播动力学和出现的影响,强调病毒学机制和“一体化健康”准备工作。(A2)
analysis_zh.current_state: 汉坦病毒es 已广泛多样化并适应多种宿主,包括啮齿动物、蝙蝠、爬行动物和鱼类,其中啮齿动物是主要的自然储存宿主。(A3)
analysis_zh.gaps: 迫切需要将病毒学准备工作与不断变化的环境条件相匹配,凸显当前基因组监测和综合“一体化健康”框架的不足。(A10)
analysis_zh.future_research: 构建将生态、病毒学和公共卫生监测相结合的概念框架,有助于预测未来气候相关的 汉坦病毒 暴发。(A9)
